direct.name: NILEQ
direct.product_name: NILEQ "Resilient Absolute Positioning" (terrain-fingerprinting navigation module, co-developed/integrated with Advanced Navigation's resilient INS)
direct.mechanism: NILEQ uses patent-pending neuromorphic ("event-based") camera sensors that, instead of capturing full image frames, track per-pixel brightness changes as the airborne platform flies over terrain. This stream is processed to derive a "terrain fingerprint," which is matched in real time against an existing pre-loaded database/map of the Earth's surface (a geospatial reference dataset, analogous to scene/terrain-referenced map-matching). When a match is found, the system outputs an absolute position fix that is fed into the platform's navigation system to correct INS drift — explicitly removing the need for GPS. This is a genuine map-matching / scene-matching absolute positioning mechanism (same job as OSCAR/Flyby), not pure relative VIO/SLAM and not pure inertial dead-reckoning. It is positioned as a module/sensor that complements (feeds corrections into) an inertial navigation system (e.g., Advanced Navigation's INS), similar to how Flyby/OSCAR are described as modules feeding absolute fixes into a host nav stack.
direct.accuracy: n/d — no specific meter-level accuracy figure was found in any public source (multiple sources explicitly confirm this is not yet publicly disclosed)
direct.day_night_jamming: Sources describe the solution as "passive" and "resistant to interference," explicitly designed to provide a position fix when GPS is jammed or spoofed in contested/congested electromagnetic environments. No explicit public statement found confirming night-time operation capability of the neuromorphic camera (event-based sensors are typically high-dynamic-range and often marketed for low-light performance, but this was not explicitly confirmed for NILEQ in available sources) — treat day/night claim as not directly disclosed (n/d on night specifically), while jamming/spoofing resilience is clearly and repeatedly claimed across sources.

In November 2024, MBDA and Advanced Navigation (Australian INS maker) signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) to co-develop a resilient navigation system integrating NILEQ's absolute positioning technology, with plans for an airborne demonstration in Australia (originally targeted for 2025, under the AUKUS technology-sharing framework). direct.name: Daedalean (acquired by Destinus, Jan 2026)
direct.website: https://www.daedalean.ai (now a subsidiary of Destinus, https://www.destinus.com)
direct.product_name: Visual Positioning System (VPS), comprising Visual Global Positioning System (VGPS) + Visual Motion Unit (VMU); also marketed as part of Daedalean's "Visual Navigation" / GNSS-independent positioning suite
direct.mechanism: Yes — matches live camera imagery to a pre-loaded reference. Daedalean's VGPS requires a pre-built database/map of georeferenced landmarks (visual feature descriptors with 3D positions in the WGS84 frame, derived from a prior survey/satellite-type map). In flight, the onboard camera detects landscape features and matches them against this pre-loaded landmark map to fix absolute global position, without GNSS. This "global localization" (VGPS) is fused with a real-time but drift-prone "local localization" SLAM/VIO layer (VMU) to produce a continuous, accurate absolute position output in real time. This is architecturally the same job as OSCAR/Flyby: camera-to-pre-loaded-map matching to yield absolute coordinates, with VIO/SLAM only as the complementary short-term layer, not the primary fix. The system tolerates landscape change (e.g., seasonal differences) as long as roughly 10%+ of landmarks still match the original survey map.
direct.accuracy: Stated as 4% of height-above-ground-level (HAGL) horizontal and 3% HAGL vertical; example given: flying at 500 m altitude yields ~20 m horizontal / ~15 m vertical accuracy. This is consistent with (slightly looser than) the OSCAR/Flyby reference band of ~5-30 m, scaling with altitude.
direct.day_night_jamming: Marketed explicitly as a GNSS-independent/backup positioning source designed to function "when GNSS is denied" (jamming/spoofing/outage scenarios) — this GPS-denied/backup framing is the company's central value proposition across its navigation product pages and blog posts. Sources consistently describe it as working from passive camera/landscape imagery (no day/night-specific limitation stated in the sources found, consistent with EO camera-based operation; no explicit "works at night" marketing claim was found in available excerpts, so this should be treated as not fully documented — note as a gap).

direct.name: Spleenlab
direct.product_name: VISIONAIRY® Suite — specifically the "GPS-Denied Navigation" capability built from two combined modules: Visual-Inertial Odometry (VIO) and Map-Based Relocalization (IR | EO)
direct.mechanism: Spleenlab's GPS-denied navigation combines two fused modules. (1) Visual-Inertial Odometry (VIO): onboard RGB/EO and thermal/IR cameras + IMU produce continuous relative motion/pose estimation — this part alone is the classic relative-only SLAM/VIO mechanism (ADJACENT-type). (2) Map-Based Relocalization (IR|EO): the company's own product page states this module "enables precise position estimation by matching camera imagery to satellite imagery," letting the platform "reconnect to known reference maps to correct drift and maintain localization accuracy over long missions" using a pre-loaded/known reference map — i.e., it matches live camera imagery against a PRE-LOADED satellite/digital map to recover an ABSOLUTE position and correct VIO drift, exactly the OSCAR/Flyby job description. Spleenlab markets the two together as its core "GPS-Denied Navigation" defense product (VISIONAIRY®), explicitly pitched for land/air/sea defense, with onboard real-time processing on embedded hardware (NVIDIA Jetson, Qualcomm Snapdragon, TI TDA4VM), no cloud/ground dependency. Separately, Spleenlab/team published a SPRIN-D "Kilometer-Scale GNSS-Denied UAV Navigation" challenge-winning system that matches LiDAR-derived local heightmaps to a prior geodata heightmap via gradient-template matching, fused with odometry in a particle filter — reinforcing that map/terrain-matching to a pre-loaded reference (not just relative VIO) is core to their approach and competitive identity. Because the flagship, marketed "GPS-Denied Navigation" solution explicitly includes camera-to-pre-loaded-map matching for absolute position correction (not merely relative odometry), this is classified DIRECT, with the caveat that VIO/relative tracking is the primary continuous estimator and map-matching acts as a periodic absolute-correction/relocalization layer rather than a continuous map-matching positioning system like OSCAR. This is a meaningfully different architecture (VIO+periodic relocalization vs. continuous scene-matching) but performs the same core job: deriving absolute, GPS-free coordinates by matching live camera imagery to a pre-existing satellite/reference map.
direct.accuracy: No single public absolute-accuracy figure (in meters) for the Map-Based Relocalization module specifically was found on the product pages (search-engine cache only; pages return HTTP 403 to direct fetch, so this could not be independently quoted verbatim — flagged as a gap). A related but distinct figure: VISIONAIRY VIO/SLAM cites "±2.5 cm" position accuracy "in typical environments" at up to 200 Hz update rate (this is the local/relative VIO precision, not absolute geo-referenced accuracy from map-matching). Separately, the SPRIN-D Challenge-winning Spleenlab-linked terrain/heightmap-matching system achieved RMSE below 11 m over kilometer-scale GNSS-denied flights — this is the closest verified absolute-accuracy figure for their map-matching approach (terrain heightmap matching, not satellite-image matching). Treat accuracy claims with caution given inability to directly verify the primary product page text.
direct.day_night_jamming: Day/night: claimed yes — combines RGB/EO (day, high-resolution feature detection) with thermal/IR imaging explicitly for "low-light, night, or visually obscured conditions," and an "SLAM EO|IR" module fuses both for "all visibility conditions." Jamming/spoofing: company markets the GPS-denied suite as "immune to GPS jamming and spoofing, ensuring mission continuity in contested or electronically noisy environments" — since the whole pipeline (VIO + map relocalization) uses only passive optical/IR + IMU sensors with no GNSS dependency, it does not rely on RF signals that can be jammed/spoofed. These are vendor marketing claims, not independently verified test data.

direct.name: Vantor
direct.product_name: Raptor (software suite: Raptor Guide, Raptor Sync, Raptor Ace)
direct.mechanism: Raptor is a vision-based software suite that uses a drone's onboard/native camera and matches real-time captured imagery to Vantor's pre-existing global 3D terrain/satellite reference data (Vantor "Vivid Terrain," 100M+ sq km, 3m-accurate) — matching features like buildings, trees and terrain — to establish "ground truth" and output absolute aerial position and/or absolute ground target coordinates, without GPS/GNSS and without new hardware. This is a direct match to the OSCAR/Flyby pattern: live camera imagery matched to a pre-loaded map/satellite reference to fix absolute geo-coordinates. Three modules: Raptor Guide (onboard absolute aerial position), Raptor Sync (real-time georegistration of FMV feed to 3D terrain for coordinate extraction), Raptor Ace (laptop-based post/real-time target coordinate extraction from FMV). Vantor has also partnered with Niantic Spatial (using Niantic's crowdsourced visual-positioning dataset, including from Pokemon Go scans) to extend this into a unified air-to-ground absolute visual positioning system, and partnered with BAE Systems GXP to combine Raptor's map-matching with targeting in GPS-jammed environments.
direct.accuracy: Raptor Guide: <10 m RMSE absolute aerial position accuracy (all dimensions); Raptor Sync and Raptor Ace: <3 m absolute accuracy for ground coordinate extraction; underlying Vivid Terrain reference data stated as 3 m-accurate. direct.name: Inertial Labs
direct.product_name: VINS (Vision-Aided Inertial Navigation System), integrating Maxar Raptor vision-based positioning software; also sold as part of INS-NV sensor fusion platform with "VPS" (Visual Positioning System) module
direct.mechanism: Inertial Labs is fundamentally an INS/IMU/AHRS hardware company (since 2001), but its 2025-launched VINS product integrates Maxar's "Raptor" 3D vision-based positioning software: an onboard camera (day or IR) captures real-time imagery which is matched, using Perspective-n-Point (PnP) algorithms, against pre-loaded, satellite-derived Maxar Precision3D 3D mesh maps (~3m base map accuracy) to compute the vehicle's absolute 3D position without GNSS. This absolute vision-based position fix is then fused via an extended Kalman filter with the IMU/INS and a secondary ground-facing-camera visual-inertial-odometry (relative motion) input. This matches the OSCAR/Flyby pattern (camera-to-preloaded-map matching for absolute coordinates), though the core matching algorithm is licensed/integrated from Maxar/Vantor rather than developed in-house, and the product also bundles relative VIO as a secondary aid.
direct.accuracy: Demonstrated in GNSS-denied flight tests: horizontal position maintained within ~35 m, vertical within 5 m, velocity within 0.9 m/s (PR Newswire/Defense Advancement case study); separate flight-test report: CEP50 generally 5-15 m and CEP95 15-25 m over extended flight distances (one case: mean error 12.2 m, CEP50 9.31 m, CEP95 25.81 m). Base Maxar Precision3D reference maps stated as ~3 m accurate. When GNSS is available, sub-meter horizontal / ~2 m vertical.
direct.day_night_jamming: Supports both day camera and IR (night/thermal) camera inputs for the vision-positioning function. Explicitly marketed for GNSS-jammed, spoofed, and denied environments as part of Inertial Labs' "Assured PNT" (APNT) product line; VINS press materials state it is designed for "GPS-compromised flight paths" and "GNSS-challenged/contested" UAV missions.
direct.pricing: Hardware sales/B2B/defense-contractor model via direct sales and a worldwide distributor network (20+ countries, 6 continents); no public list pricing — quote-based through distributors (e.g., Aeroexpo, GIM International). VINS/INS-NV are COTS sensor-fusion modules sold as hardware (with optional COTS radio link), not a SaaS/subscription product.

In December 2024, VIAVI Solutions Inc. announced acquisition of Inertial Labs for $150 million initial consideration at closing plus up to $175 million in contingent (earn-out) consideration over four years; deal closed Q1 2025. The legacy/base layer is INS (inertial) augmented by GPS with company-made multi-element CRPA anti-jam antennas and a proprietary anti-spoofing detection algorithm, plus Time-of-Arrival (ToA) multilateration to let multiple drones navigate together without GPS (this part alone = ADJACENT, i.e., INS/anti-jam, not map-matching). This is functionally the same job as OSCAR/Flyby - visual terrain/map-matching against a pre-loaded reference to derive absolute position - making the latest-generation capability DIRECT, even though it is an embedded subsystem of their munitions rather than a standalone sold "module."

direct.name: Theseus (Theseus Technology Corporation)
direct.mechanism: Theseus's Micro VPS is a hardware+software module (camera + IMU) that compares live onboard camera imagery of the terrain below against a vast onboard database of pre-loaded satellite/reference maps (originally prototyped against Google Maps imagery, now an internal satellite-imagery database at ~0.5 m/pixel resolution) to compute absolute geographic coordinates via terrain/scene map-matching, fused with visual-inertial odometry for continuity between map-match fixes. It then outputs a simulated GPS signal (NMEA/GPS-spoofed message) to any flight controller (PX4/ArduPilot) so the autopilot believes it still has GPS. This is a direct, literal match to the OSCAR/Flyby "match live camera to pre-loaded map to get absolute coordinates without GPS" pattern -- not pure VIO/SLAM (which only gives relative motion). Company materials explicitly state the algorithm is "designed to be resilient to variations in terrain and seasonal changes... to achieve reliable absolute positioning" and that it performs well "regardless of multi-pathing, jamming, or alterations in the skyline compared to satellite maps."
direct.accuracy: Marketing/target: ~5 m (95% of time), comparable to consumer GPS. Independent/real-world flight test (564 km, 5h22m flight over central Florida, March test per Defence Blog/secondary reporting): median horizontal error of 51.95 m over the full mission with zero mid-flight reinitializations; other secondary reporting cites "20 m or less over any flight distance" in some test configurations. So stated accuracy ranges roughly 5-50+ m depending on source/test, broadly in the same order of magnitude as the 5-30 m OSCAR/Flyby benchmark but with reported real-world figures sometimes exceeding it.

Positioned explicitly as a response to GPS jamming/spoofing seen in Ukraine, Iran, and Syria conflicts.

This is relative/self-referential visual-inertial-style localization (closer to VIO/SLAM), not absolute terrain-referenced/map-matching navigation against a pre-existing satellite or digital elevation map like OSCAR/Flyby. adjacent.name: Flare Bright
adjacent.product_name: SENS (Software Enhanced Navigation System) core platform; Tactera (terrain-referenced absolute positioning add-on); Extera (flight termination/containment safety system)
adjacent.mechanism: Two distinct products, neither matches the OSCAR/Flyby pattern exactly. (1) Core SENS technology: a software "digital twin" of the airframe (aerodynamics, propulsion, fuel use) combined with machine-learning-enhanced dead reckoning that minimizes IMU/INS drift error - this is pure inertial/model-based dead reckoning with NO external reference map and NO camera; it is reset to zero error whenever GPS is briefly reacquired. This is classic INS-based GPS-denied nav (ADJACENT, not DIRECT - no absolute fix without GPS reset). (2) Newer product "Tactera" (launched 2025): pairs a low-cost automotive LIDAR sensor with a pre-loaded Digital Elevation Model (DEM)/commercial terrain elevation map of the operating area; the LIDAR measures terrain range/contour beneath the aircraft and matches it against the pre-loaded DEM to derive an absolute position fix - i.e., terrain-referenced navigation / TERCOM-style terrain contour matching. This DOES use a pre-loaded reference map to output absolute coordinates without GPS, similar in structural intent to OSCAR/Flyby, BUT the sensing modality is LIDAR range/elevation data, NOT a camera matching live optical/visual imagery to a pre-loaded satellite/photographic map. It is explicitly not vision-based: no camera, no optical scene-matching, works regardless of light or visual contrast since it depends on terrain shape, not appearance. Because the rubric defines DIRECT specifically as vision-based (camera-to-map) absolute positioning, Tactera's LIDAR-to-DEM terrain matching is a different mechanism family (terrain-referenced/TERCOM navigation) and should be classified ADJACENT, not DIRECT - it solves the same "no-GPS absolute fix via pre-loaded reference" problem but via a non-visual ranging sensor rather than a camera-based visual positioning system.
adjacent.accuracy: SENS/INS dead reckoning: accurate navigation maintained for "up to one hour" before drift requires correction (no absolute accuracy figure beyond GPS-comparable until reset). Tactera: demonstrated ~30 m accuracy in 2025 Spain flight trials; company stated plan (as of DSEI Sept 2025) to improve to ~10 m accuracy by end of December 2025.
adjacent.day_night_jamming: Tactera marketed as working "day or night" since it relies on LIDAR ranging/terrain shape rather than optical imagery (so dark/low-contrast scenes are not a limitation, unlike camera-based VPS). Described by the company as "unjammable and unspoofable" - in testing with active jammers present, reported that "the system ignored the jamming, it didn't even see it." Core SENS dead-reckoning approach is inherently immune to RF jamming/spoofing since it uses no external radio signal, and the company notes it also is not degraded by featureless terrain (desert/sea) where camera-based visual nav would fail - though Tactera's LIDAR-DEM approach would itself struggle over featureless terrain like calm open water, unlike pure inertial dead reckoning.
adjacent.pricing: No public list pricing; sells as an integrable navigation module/payload to UAV/munitions OEMs and defense primes (B2B/B2G). Tactera's bill-of-materials emphasizes low cost - the LIDAR sensor used costs around £500 and weighs ~170 g, positioned as a low-cost COTS-based system suitable for expendable/low-cost munitions and small UAS, contrasted with expensive military-grade INS. Engaged via government contracts/competitions (UK Dstl, UK MOD, US DoD SBIR-style sprints) and through partner integration trials (e.g., with Embention/BCN Drone Center).

adjacent.name: Roke
adjacent.product_name: RENS (visual-inertial navigation system); also eLORAN/Nav-Sync Pulse/MILOR (RF-based terrestrial PNT) within Roke's broader "GPS-Denied Navigation" capability
adjacent.mechanism: Roke's flagship GPS-denied navigation product, RENS, is a visual-inertial odometry (VIO) system: a single camera + IMU + a small onboard processor (Raspberry Pi-class hardware) track frame-to-frame visual motion fused with inertial data to estimate RELATIVE position/pose as the platform moves. Roke explicitly markets its performance as a "drift rate" (sub-4% drift over 2km during hour-long missions, 10Hz output) — drift is a metric meaningful only for relative dead-reckoning systems, not for absolute map-matched positioning (an absolute fix would not "drift" with distance/time). There is no evidence in Roke's public materials that RENS, or any other Roke product, matches live camera imagery against a PRE-LOADED digital/satellite reference map or terrain database to output absolute geo-coordinates (no TERCOM/terrain-relative-navigation-style scene-matching language anywhere on Roke's site or in secondary coverage). Roke's wider "GPS-Denied Navigation" / PNT portfolio is a grab-bag of DIFFERENT mechanisms rather than one OSCAR/Flyby-style module: RENS (VIO, vision+inertial, relative), plus eLORAN-based terrestrial RF positioning/timing products (Nav-Sync Pulse miniature eLoran antenna/receiver, MILOR eLoran receiver) which use low-frequency ground RF signals, not camera/map correlation, for resilient PNT. This mixed bag of VIO + RF-eLoran is squarely the "different mechanism" case the rubric calls ADJACENT, not the camera-to-pre-loaded-map absolute fix that defines DIRECT/OSCAR/Flyby.
adjacent.accuracy: RENS: sub-4% positional drift over 2km during hour-long indoor/outdoor missions (a relative-drift metric, not an absolute fix accuracy in meters); 10Hz position update rate. No "absolute accuracy in meters" figure (e.g. 5-30m CEP) is published, consistent with it not being an absolute map-matched system.
adjacent.day_night_jamming: RENS camera has NIR sensitivity and is optimized for active IR illumination, enabling low-light/night operation. RENS works wherever there are sufficient visual features (buildings, tunnels, underground facilities, GPS-denied indoor/outdoor environments) since it is camera+IMU based and not reliant on RF signals at all, making it inherently immune to RF jamming/spoofing (it simply doesn't use GNSS). Roke's separate eLORAN-based products (Nav-Sync Pulse, MILOR) are explicitly marketed as jam/spoof-resistant alternatives to GPS using high-power, low-frequency terrestrial RF signals "exceptionally difficult" to jam or spoof at range. No specific day/night/jamming claims were found tied to a camera-to-map absolute positioning product, because Roke does not appear to sell one.
adjacent.pricing: No public pricing; Roke operates as a UK defence/national-security R&D and engineering contractor delivering bespoke systems, products and contract R&D to government and commercial customers (not a SaaS/subscription model). Business model is contract-based (government PNT contracts, e.g. UK government eLoran contract) plus product sales (e.g. Nav-Sync Pulse antenna, MILOR receiver) to defence/maritime customers.
adjacent.funding_detail: Roke is not a startup and has no VC funding rounds. It was founded in 1956 by Plessey, became Roke Manor Research under a GEC-Siemens joint venture (1990), passed to full Siemens ownership (1991), and was acquired by Chemring Group PLC in 2010 for approximately GBP 55 million. Chemring Group is a publicly listed UK defence company (LSE, FTSE 250), and Roke operates as a wholly-owned subsidiary/business unit of Chemring.
adjacent.investors: Parent company: Chemring Group PLC (LSE-listed, FTSE 250) -- corporate ownership, not venture investors.
adjacent.traction: Roke has been awarded a UK government contract for eLoran-based resilient PNT (part of a wider GBP 155 million UK government investment in eLoran/timing/GNSS-monitoring resilience). Roke publishes RENS as a deployable product for tactical/defence GPS-denied indoor and unmanned-vehicle navigation, and miniaturized eLoran products (Nav-Sync Pulse, MILOR) for defence and maritime customers, but no independent UAV-platform integration deals or unit-sales traction figures were found in public sources.
adjacent.strategy_stage: Established UK defence/national-security R&D house (not an early-stage startup); positioning itself as a multi-pronged resilient-PNT provider, combining VIO (RENS), RF-based eLoran timing/positioning, and AI/sensor-fusion R&D, plus broader EW/comms/AI/cyber capabilities, rather than a single dedicated absolute visual-map-matching navigation module like OSCAR/Flyby.

adjacent.name: Exail Technologies
adjacent.product_name: Advans Series / Ursa U5 (and broader FOG-based INS/AHRS product range)
adjacent.mechanism: Exail's GNSS-denied navigation solutions (Advans Series, Ursa U5, and the rapidly-deployable GNSS-denied kit launched in 2026) are built entirely on fiber-optic gyroscope (FOG) inertial navigation/dead-reckoning technology, not vision-based map-matching. There is no evidence in any product page, press release, or third-party article that Exail matches live camera imagery against a pre-loaded digital/satellite map to compute absolute coordinates. Accuracy is instead expressed as inertial drift relative to distance traveled (e.g., 0.1% DT, 0.4% DT for Ursa U5) plus azimuth accuracy (0.5 mil) — the classic signature of pure INS dead-reckoning, which accumulates error over time/distance rather than fixing an absolute position via terrain/scene matching. This does NOT match the OSCAR/Flyby pattern (camera-to-pre-loaded-map absolute positioning); it is a different mechanism category (pure INS/FOG), explicitly excluded as ADJACENT by the classification rubric.
adjacent.accuracy: Drift-based, not fixed accuracy: ~0.1% of Distance Traveled (Advans Series) and ~0.4% DT (Ursa U5), with 0.5 mil azimuth accuracy — error grows with distance/time since there is no absolute map-match correction, unlike OSCAR/Flyby's ~5-30 m absolute fix.
adjacent.day_night_jamming: Marketed explicitly as resilient to GNSS jamming/spoofing/denial (works without any satellite signal at all, since it is inertial, not GNSS or camera/light dependent) — inherently day/night capable because FOG gyros do not rely on optical imagery. adjacent.mechanism: AQNav does NOT use a camera/optical sensor matched to a satellite/visual reference map. It uses extremely sensitive quantum magnetometers to measure Earth's crustal (geomagnetic) magnetic field, which has geographically unique, location-specific anomaly patterns ("a magnetic fingerprint"). AI algorithms compare the live magnetometer readings against a pre-loaded database/map of known magnetic-field signatures to determine absolute position — this is magnetic anomaly map-matching (MagNav), analogous in structure (live sensor reading vs. pre-loaded reference map -> absolute fix) to terrain-referenced navigation, but using the magnetic spectrum instead of visible-light camera imagery. No camera or visual scene-matching is involved at all, so it fails the OSCAR/Flyby DIRECT criterion of "matches live camera imagery to a pre-loaded digital/satellite map."

adjacent.name: Near Earth Autonomy
adjacent.product_name: Firefly (Miniaturized/Compact Autonomy System); core GPS-denied tech originally branded as a SLAM-based autonomy stack (also used on K-MAX TITAN, KARGO UAV, FVR-90, TRV-150)
adjacent.mechanism: Near Earth Autonomy's GPS-denied navigation is built on Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM), fused with LiDAR, infrared, and HD camera sensing. Per NASA's own Spinoff article (NASA funded the core SBIR R&D): "the drone builds a map of its surroundings while tracking its own movement through that environment" -- i.e., the vehicle constructs its own map on the fly and localizes RELATIVE to that self-built map/odometry chain. This is NOT the OSCAR/Flyby pattern: there is no public evidence the system matches live camera imagery against a PRE-LOADED satellite/digital reference map to output absolute, drift-free geo-coordinates. Marketing language ("with or without GPS," autonomous landing-zone/hazard detection without pre-mapped flight paths) and product literature (Firefly: LiDAR + IR + HD camera for hazard/obstacle detection and confined-area landing) consistently describe relative perception/SLAM and obstacle avoidance, not absolute terrain-referenced/scene-matching positioning. No accuracy figures, no day/night absolute-fix claims, and no jamming/spoofing-resilience-via-map-match claims were found anywhere in company materials or press coverage -- the jamming/EMCON resilience they cite (e.g., the NAVAIR maritime logistics contract) comes from not needing GPS at all (dead-reckoning/SLAM/vision-based relative nav + sensor fusion), not from re-anchoring to a stored reference map the way OSCAR/Flyby do. This places Near Earth Autonomy squarely in the ADJACENT category: GPS-denied navigation via a different mechanism (SLAM/visual-inertial + LiDAR relative localization and obstacle-aware autonomy), not absolute vision map-matching.

adjacent.name: The Fourth Law (TFL)
adjacent.product_name: TFL-1 autonomy module (terminal guidance / "AI co-pilot" for FPV drones)
adjacent.mechanism: TFL-1 does NOT match live camera imagery to a pre-loaded digital/satellite map to compute absolute coordinates. It is a computer-vision-based "fire-and-forget" TERMINAL GUIDANCE / target-lock system: during the final ~400-500 m of an FPV strike, the onboard AI visually detects an operator-selected target (stationary or moving), locks onto it, and autonomously flies the drone to the target center, independent of GNSS and resilient to loss of the radio control link/EW jamming of the video/control signal. This is target-relative visual servoing/guidance, not absolute self-localization against a reference map. The company's own public 5-stage roadmap lists "GPS-denied navigation" (full cruise/waypoint navigation without GNSS) as a separate, FUTURE roadmap stage beyond the currently shipped terminal-guidance and target-selection capabilities -- i.e., even TFL's own framing distinguishes what's shipped (vision target-lock) from absolute GPS-denied navigation, which is not yet delivered/described as map-matching. No source (company site sections fetched were blocked by 403, but multiple independent press write-ups corroborate consistently) describes scene-matching to a pre-loaded satellite/terrain database to output geo-coordinates. Therefore this is GPS-independent terminal guidance/visual target-lock, not a VPS/terrain-referenced absolute positioning module -- classified ADJACENT (GPS-denied capability, but different mechanism than OSCAR/Flyby's map-matching).

Because the mechanism is RF time-of-flight (a different physical principle than visual map-matching), this does not meet the DIRECT bar of OSCAR/Flyby-style visual terrain-referenced navigation.

adjacent.mechanism: Swarmer is a swarm coordination / autonomy software platform, not a visual absolute-positioning module. Per the company's own description: the software does not itself compute position from camera-to-map matching. Instead it is agnostic to the positioning source -- it "accepts the output" of whatever each drone's onboard system reports (GNSS, inertial navigation/INS, "visual cues," or other sensors), then shares that positional information across the swarm via mesh networking so the group has collective situational awareness. If one drone briefly regains a GNSS fix, a "visual landmark match," or a beacon signal, that higher-confidence data point can propagate to stabilize the rest of the formation. This is a multi-source sensor-fusion/information-sharing approach to resilience (collective redundancy across a swarm), not a dedicated vision module that matches live camera imagery against a pre-loaded satellite/terrain map to output absolute geo-coordinates the way OSCAR/Flyby does. No product page, datasheet, or article found describes a terrain-referenced/scene-matching visual navigation engine as Swarmer's core sold capability; its three products (STYX, MINAS, TRIDENT) are command-and-control, multi-drone autonomy/coordination AI, and an embedded drone OS, respectively -- a broader autonomy/orchestration platform, which per the classification rubric falls under ADJACENT even if "visual landmark match" is mentioned as one possible input source.
